text: For a smallholder farmer in Preah Vihear, selling live poultry depends on bird type, flock size, age, condition, buyer demand, feed cost, transport cost, and disease risk. Channels include farm-gate buyers, village traders/collectors, local markets, restaurants, slaughterers, or direct sale. A farmer with few birds may find a farm-gate buyer more practical since the buyer handles transport and the farmer avoids market fees and handling. Costs include feed, mortality, transport, cages, market fees, labor, and rejected birds — compare net return, not just price per bird. Live-bird markets create real transmission risk for avian influenza and Newcastle disease because birds from different farms mix — sick birds, birds from a flock with unexplained deaths, or birds showing serious respiratory/neurological signs should never be transported to market. During the wet season (roughly May–October), rain, muddy roads, and wet cages complicate transport and hygiene; during the dry season (roughly November–April), heat stress, dehydration, and dust during transport matter more. For eggs, prioritize cleanliness, shell condition, freshness, and heat protection over trying to replicate a live-bird marketing system. No specific chicken breed is assumed dominant in Preah Vihear without local evidence — record the farmer's actual bird type and source. Group marketing can reduce transport cost per bird but increases biosecurity risk from mixing flocks, so buyers collecting separately from individual farms is safer than combining live birds.
